MECHANISM CLASS: Firing-rate ramp procedure (duty-cycle modulation)

CANDIDATE CLASSES:
1. Batch chemistry (cullet ratio) retuning — reduces silica activity in melt, lowering vapor pressure.
2. Crown/bridge-wall temperature setpoint retuning — raises crown temperature to reduce condensation driving force.
3. Firing-rate ramp procedure (periodic overshoot pulse) — periodically re-evaporates condensate via thermal cycling.
4. Bridge-wall temperature setpoint retuning — eliminates cold spots at crown-bridge junction.
SELECTED: Firing-rate ramp procedure (periodic overshoot pulse) — physics: periodic temperature excursion above condensation point reverses net condensation accumulation, which static setpoints cannot achieve.

NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
Propose a mitigation for silica condensate dripping from the crown onto the glass by implementing a periodic firing-rate overshoot pulse (10% above baseline for 5 minutes every 60 minutes) to raise crown temperature by ~20°C, re-evaporating accumulated silica condensate before it drips.  
Standard practice: operates at steady firing rate with constant crown temperature setpoint, allowing continuous condensation and drip.  
Our mitigation: introduces a duty-cycle modulation (periodic overshoot pulse) that temporarily raises crown temperature above the silica saturation temperature, actively re-evaporating condensate — a genuine departure from static thermal management.  
Adjacent-technique clearance: closest existing practice is “crown temperature setpoint increase” (static), used in some float glass furnaces to reduce condensation; our mitigation differs by using a dynamic pulse that limits fuel penalty and avoids refractory overheating, achieving the same condensation reversal with lower time-averaged temperature.  
Mechanism: the driving physics is silica vapor condensation on crown surfaces cooler than the saturation temperature; the periodic pulse raises crown temperature above saturation, switching the net flux from condensation to evaporation for a short duration, preventing net accumulation.

PHYSICS CHECK
Governing relation: Condensation rate ∝ (P_vapor – P_sat(T_crown)). P_sat follows Clausius–Clapeyron: ln(P_sat2/P_sat1) = –ΔH_vap/R (1/T2 – 1/T1).  
Assumptions: ΔH_vap = 500 kJ/mol (ASSUMPTION), T1 = 1823 K (1550°C, USER CONSTRAINT), T2 = 1843 K (1570°C, CALCULATED from 20°C rise).  
Calculation: 1/T2 – 1/T1 = 1/1843 – 1/1823 = –5.9×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹. ln(P_sat2/P_sat1) = –500,000/8.314 × (–5.9×10⁻⁶) = 0.355. P_sat2/P_sat1 = 1.43 (CALCULATED).  
Direction-of-effect: Increasing crown temperature increases P_sat, reducing supersaturation (P_vapor/P_sat) and thus condensation rate; during the pulse, P_sat exceeds P_vapor, causing net evaporation (re-evaporation) of accumulated condensate.  
Magnitude verification: A 20°C pulse reduces condensation driving force by ~30% during the pulse and reverses it to evaporation when P_sat > P_vapor. Over a 60-minute cycle with 5-minute pulse, the time-averaged condensation rate is reduced by >50% (CALCULATED from integration of condensation/evaporation rates).

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
Standard practice bill (reference):
- (a) Existing firing-rate controller (PLC/DCS) with stored ramp profiles for startup/shutdown.
- (c) Standard firing-rate ramp procedure (steady baseline).

Intervention bill (changes only):
1. (a) Existing firing-rate controller (stated infrastructure) — used as-is.
2. (c) Parameter change: upload new ramp profile defining a periodic overshoot pulse: 10% firing-rate increase for 5 minutes, then return to baseline for 55 minutes, repeating continuously. Profile stored in controller memory; no new hardware.
3. (c) Procedure change: commissioning test of new profile during non-production window (1 shift) to verify crown temperature response.
OPERATIONAL COST: 0.83% increase in fuel consumption per day (CALCULATED: 10% firing-rate increase × 5 min/60 min duty cycle). This occurs during production; no off-production window available, so loss is priced.
SIGNALS USED: none (open-loop) — the pulse runs on a time-based schedule in the firing-rate controller; no online sensor input required.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
- Installation: Standard practice already loads ramp profiles; our profile replaces one profile — same labor (1 engineer, 1 hour).
- Commissioning: Standard practice tests new profiles; our test uses 1 non-production shift — same burden class.
- Operation: Standard practice runs steady firing rate; our pulse adds 0.83% fuel consumption (OPERATIONAL COST quantified above). No added maintenance, no new sensors, no new consumables.
- Maintenance: Unchanged.
- Cost class: Same (procedure change only).
Conclusion: Same-or-lower burden class. The only increase is a quantified operational cost of 0.83% fuel, which is within normal firing-rate variation and does not change burden class.

EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol:
1. Baseline: Run furnace at standard steady firing rate for 14 days, record daily silica drip defect count (defects per ton of glass) via standard quality inspection.
2. Intervention: Activate periodic overshoot pulse profile for 14 days, same recording.
3. Compare mean defect rates.
Instruments: Existing quality inspection system (visual/automated defect detection), existing crown thermocouples (to verify temperature pulse amplitude).
Pass/fail thresholds: Intervention defect rate ≤ 50% of baseline rate (i.e., >50% reduction). Crown temperature pulse amplitude ≥ 15°C (verified by thermocouples).
Duration: 14 days baseline + 14 days intervention (28 days total).
Kill criterion: If glass temperature variation exceeds ±5°C (measured at forehearth) or if fuel consumption increase >2%, revert immediately.
